links.note: 751 says nothing but wealth turns people who count for nothing into people who count (பொருளல்லவரைப் பொருளாகச் செய்யும்). 973 says those who are not high are not high even when seated high (மேலிருந்தும் மேலல்லார் மேலல்லர்). They conflict if 751 is read as wealth conferring real worth; on Parimelazhagar's reading, where wealth only makes the unregarded regarded by others, the two can stand together.

751 ends by saying there is no பொருள் other than wealth that lifts the worthless (பொருளல்லது இல்லை பொருள்). 400 says learning is the imperishable wealth and other things are not wealth at all (மாடல்ல மற்றையவை). Each gives the title of the one real wealth to a different thing, so on a literal reading the two exclusive claims cannot both hold.

751 treats wealth's power to give standing to persons of no account as its distinction. 241 notes the same fact, that material wealth is found even among the base (பொருட்செல்வம் பூரியார் கண்ணும் உள), and uses it to rank wealth below grace, the 'wealth among wealths'. What 751 counts in wealth's favour, 241 counts against it.

752 says everyone scorns those who have nothing (இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர்). 1046 gives a particular case: even when the poor understand a good matter well and say it, their words go slack (சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும்). The general contempt of 752 is shown reaching what a poor person says.

752's 'everyone' (எல்லாரும்) scorns the have-nots. 1047 carries that to the limit case: one in poverty not joined to virtue is looked on as a stranger even by the mother who bore him (ஈன்ற தாயானும் பிறன்போல). The pairing shows how far 'everyone' reaches, with 1047 adding the condition அறஞ்சாரா.

752 reports that all scorn the poor and all honour the rich. 988 says lack is no disgrace to one who has the firmness called worth (இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று சால்பென்னும் திண்மை). 752 describes how the world behaves; 988 denies that the scorn is deserved where character is present, which Parimelazhagar's gloss on 752 (scorned 'even if they have every good') makes pointed.

753 calls wealth the unfailing lamp (பொய்யா விளக்கம்) that cuts away darkness in any country one thinks of. 299 says not all lamps are lamps and that for the worthy the பொய்யா விளக்கு, the lamp of not lying, is the lamp. The same phrase is given to wealth in the book of polity and to truthfulness in the book of virtue.

753 says the lamp of wealth goes to whatever country one has in mind (எண்ணிய தேயத்துச் சென்று) and removes the darkness there. 397 says that for the learned any country and any town is their own (யாதானும் நாடாமால் ஊராமால்). Wealth and learning are each described as something that works beyond one's own land.

753 says wealth cuts away darkness (இருளறுக்கும்), which Parimelazhagar takes to be enmity. 759 says no steel is sharper than wealth for cutting the pride of foes (செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும்). Both use the verb அறு for what wealth does, once as a lamp and once as a blade; on Parimelazhagar's reading of 753 they make the same claim.

754 says wealth that came by knowing the right means and without wrong yields virtue and also pleasure (அறன்ஈனும் இன்பமும் ஈனும்). 39 says only what comes through virtue is pleasure (அறத்தான் வருவதே இன்பம்). 754 fits wealth into 39's rule: wealth produces real pleasure only when it was itself acquired without wrong.

754 has blameless wealth give birth to virtue (அறன் ஈனும்). 31 has virtue give birth to distinction and to wealth (செல்வமும் ஈனும்). The same verb ஈனும் runs in both directions, so the pairing shows virtue and rightly got wealth each producing the other.

754 limits its promise to wealth that came without wrong (தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள்). 659 says what was taken making others weep leaves with weeping, while what came by good ways pays later even if lost (பிற்பயக்கும் நற்பாலவை). Both make the manner of acquisition decide what wealth yields.

755 says a gain of wealth that does not come with grace and love should be let go, not embraced (புல்லார் புரள விடல்). 113 says gain that comes from leaving fairness should be let go that very day even if it brings only good (அன்றே யொழிய விடல்). Both end on the same command, விடல், for gain acquired the wrong way, one naming love and grace as the test and the other fairness.

755 tells one to refuse wealth that comes without grace and love. 1009 says what becomes of such wealth: bright wealth amassed by setting love aside and not looking to virtue (அன்பொரீஇ ... அறநோக்காது ஈட்டிய) is taken by others. 1009 supplies a consequence for the wealth 755 rejects.

755 rejects wealth gathered without grace and love. 660 says making wealth by deceit and thinking it safe is like pouring water into an unfired clay pot (பசுமண் கலத்துள் நீர்). Parimelazhagar's note on 755 uses this same image, saying such wealth perishes and takes its maker with it, so he reads 755 through 660.

756 lists what is the king's wealth: what falls to him, customs dues, and what he takes from crushed enemies (உறுபொருளும் உல்கு பொருளும் ... தெறுபொருளும்). 552 says a sceptre-holder's demand is like a man with a spear saying 'hand it over' (வேலொடு நின்றான் இடுவென்றது). 756's sources are dues and enemies; 552 marks the limit, that exacting from one's own subjects is robbery.

385 says a king is one able to create wealth, gather it, guard it and apportion it (இயற்றலும் ஈட்டலும் காத்தலும் ... வகுத்தலும்). 756 names the sources from which that wealth is to come. 756 fills in the first two terms of 385's list.

757 says the child grace, born of love, is reared by the nurse called wealth (பொருளென்னும் செல்வச் செவிலி). 247 sets the two side by side: that world is not for those without grace, as this world is not for those without wealth. Both pair அருள் with பொருள்; 247 keeps them parallel, while 757 makes grace depend on wealth to grow.

757 makes wealth the nurse without whom grace does not thrive. 241 ranks grace as the wealth among wealths because material wealth is found even among the base (பூரியார் கண்ணும் உள). Read together, wealth is needed for grace to be raised but does not produce it: love is the mother in 757, and 241 shows wealth present where grace is absent.

757 says grace is raised by wealth. 755, in the same chapter, says wealth that does not come with grace and love (அருளொடும் அன்பொடும் வாரா) is to be let go. The dependence runs both ways: grace needs wealth, but only wealth that itself came with grace and love.

758 says doing a task with something in one's own hand (தன்கைத்தொன்று உண்டாக) is like watching an elephant fight from a hilltop, which Parimelazhagar explains as acting without fear or strain. 449 says those without capital have no profit (முதலிலார்க்கு ஊதியம் இல்லை). Both make resources in hand the precondition of an undertaking; 758 adds the safety they give.

758 praises acting with wealth in hand (கைத்து உண்டாக). 593 says those who hold steady energy as what is in their hand (ஊக்கம் ஒருவந்தம் கைத்துடையார்) do not grieve that they have lost their gains. The same word கைத்து is used for money in 758 and for drive in 593, which treats energy as the holding that matters when the money is gone.

759 says to make wealth, since no steel is sharper for cutting the pride of foes (செறுநர் செருக்கறுக்கும்). 878 says the pride found in enemies dies (மாயும் பகைவர்கண் பட்ட செருக்கு) when one knows the way, builds oneself up and guards oneself (தற்செய்து தற்காப்ப). Both aim at the enemy's செருக்கு; Parimelazhagar glosses 878's தற்செய்து as enlarging oneself, and 759 names wealth as the means.

759 says wealth is sharper than any steel against foes. 546 says it is not the spear that gives victory but the king's sceptre, if it does not bend (வேலன்று வென்றி தருவது). In both the literal weapon is set below something else, wealth in one and just rule in the other.

759 calls wealth the sharpest steel (எஃகு) against enemies' pride. 985 says bowing is the weapon (படை) by which the worthy turn their opponents (மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை). Each names a non-military thing as the real weapon against foes: resources for the ruler, humility for the person of character.

760 says that for those who have made bright wealth in full, the other two, virtue and pleasure, are easy to have together (ஏனை இரண்டும் ஒருங்கு). 754 says the wealth that yields virtue and pleasure is wealth that came without wrong (தீதின்றி வந்த பொருள்). 754 supplies the condition; Parimelazhagar reads it into 760's ஒண்பொருள் as wealth that comes by the right way.

760 says abundant wealth makes virtue and pleasure easy to get. 1002 calls it a delusion to hoard without giving on the thought that everything comes from wealth (பொருளானாம் எல்லாமென்று ஈயாது இவறும் மருள்), and says it leads to a low birth. 760's claim holds for wealth that is made and used; held back by a miser, the same belief is called delusion.

760 makes wealth the route to the other two aims, virtue and pleasure. 31 makes virtue the source of distinction and wealth (சிறப்பு ஈனும் செல்வமும் ஈனும்). Each verse, speaking from within its own book, puts its own aim first as the one from which the others follow.

761 says a conquering army, complete in its parts and unafraid of wounds, is the chief of all a king's wealth (வெறுக்கையுள் எல்லாம் தலை). 381 lists the six things a king must have and puts the army first (படைகுடி கூழ் ...). The placing in 381's list and the ranking in 761 agree.

761 counts the army as a form of the king's wealth (வெறுக்கை). 759 counts wealth as a weapon, the sharpest steel against foes (எஃகு). The two neighbouring chapters describe each thing in terms of the other: wealth is a weapon and the army is wealth.

762 says the hardness that does not fear harm in a time of decline (தொலைவிடத்து) is found only in an old army (தொல்படை). 806 says those who keep to the bounds do not give up, even in decline (தொலைவிடத்தும்), the bond of those who stood by them of old (தொல்லைக்கண் நின்றார்). Both use the same two words to tie loyalty in bad times to length of standing, in an army and in friendship.

762 says only a long-established army stays firm when it is reduced and the king is faltering. 955 says an old family (பழங்குடி) does not part from its nature even when its means of giving have shrunk. In both, age of standing is what keeps character intact under loss.

762 says steadfastness in defeat is rare except in an old army (தொல்படை). 764 defines an army by courage that has come down to it (வழிவந்த வன்கண்), along with not collapsing and not being turned by subversion. 764 makes a requirement of what 762 observes, and both use வன்கண் for the quality.

763 asks what it matters if an enemy host of rats roars like the sea, since it perishes when the cobra breathes (நாகம் உயிர்ப்பக் கெடும்). 599 says the elephant, though huge and sharp-tusked, fears when a tiger attacks. Both use animals to say that number or bulk does not decide a fight; 599 names the deciding thing as drive (ஊக்கம்), its chapter's subject.

763 says a crowd of weak enemies is nothing to one strong fighter. 873 says one who, being alone, takes on the enmity of many is more foolish than the mad (தமியனாய்ப் பல்லார் பகைகொள்பவன்). 763 holds only where the one is a cobra and the many are rats; 873 is the warning for a lone person who assumes that.

764 requires an army that cannot be turned by subversion (அறைபோகாது). 747 requires a fort that cannot be taken by siege, by assault or by அறைப்படுத்தல், working on those inside. The same word names the same danger in both: an army and a fort are each judged partly by resistance to being bought or undermined from within.

764 says an army has courage that has come down to it (வழிவந்த வன்கண்). 766 lists the four things that protect an army: valour, honour, walking the excellent path of those before (மாண்ட வழிச்செலவு) and தேற்றம். 766 spells out the inherited quality of 764 as following the path of earlier warriors, which is how Parimelazhagar reads வழிச்செலவு.

765 says an army has the power (ஆற்றல்) to stand together and face even Death coming at it in rage (கூற்றுடன்று மேல்வரினும்). 269 says that for those who have attained the power of austerity (நோற்றலின் ஆற்றல்), even leaping past Death (கூற்றம் குதித்தல்) becomes possible. Both measure a strength by setting it against கூற்று, the soldier's and the ascetic's.

765 praises an army that faces Death itself. 894 says that for the weak to harm the strong is like beckoning Death with the hand (கூற்றத்தைக் கையால் விளித்தற்று). Standing firm when Death comes is valour in 765, while calling it down on oneself without the strength to answer is folly in 894; both verses turn on ஆற்றல், present in one case and absent in the other.

766 names valour and honour (மறம் மானம்) first among the four things that protect an army. 384 defines the king as one who keeps an honour that does not stray from valour (மறனிழுக்கா மானம்). The same pair is asked of the army and of its king.

no_link_reason: The verse is a tactical definition (holding the enemy's van and advancing in formation); I found no verse elsewhere that it clearly connects to beyond the chapter's shared topic.

links.note: 768 says an army gains stature through its array (படைத்தகையால் பாடு பெறும்) even if it lacks striking power and endurance; Parimelazhagar takes படைத்தகை as splendour of appearance. 750 says a fort, whatever excellences it has, is as nothing with people who lack excellence in action (வினைமாட்சி இல்லார்கண் இல்லது). They conflict if 768's பாடு is read as real military worth; if it means only repute, 768 is a concession and 750 still stands.

768 allows an army without strength to gain stature from its bearing. 273 says one without strength putting on the form of the strong (வலியில் நிலைமையான் வல்லுருவம்) is like a cow grazing in a tiger's skin. On Parimelazhagar's reading of படைத்தகை as outward show, 768 credits what 273 mocks; 273 is about a false ascetic, so the conflict holds only if both are taken as claims about appearance without substance.

769 says an army wins if it is free of dwindling, of resentment that does not leave, and of poverty (வறுமை). 759 says to make wealth because it is the sharpest weapon against foes. Parimelazhagar links them from both sides: under 769 he says desertion and want arise when the king does not pay, and under 759 that making wealth brings a large army.

769 names a resentment that will not leave (செல்லாத் துனி) among the things an army must be free of to win; Parimelazhagar says it arises from degrading treatment. 567 says harsh words and punishment beyond bounds are a file that wears down a king's conquering strength (அடுமுரண் தேய்க்கும் அரம்). 567 gives a cause on the king's side for the condition 769 warns of.

770 says that even with many steadfast men there is no army where there are no leaders (தலைமக்கள் இல்வழி இல்). 740 says a land that has attained every excellence is of no use if it has no accord with its king (வேந்தமைவில்லாத நாடு). Each chapter closes by making all its listed merits depend on the head.

770 says men without leaders are no army. 750 says a fort with every excellence is no fort with those who lack excellence in action (இல்லார்கண் இல்லது அரண்). The chapters on fort and army end on the same pattern, but point in opposite directions: the fort needs capable men inside it, the men need capable leaders.

770 says an army does not exist without leaders. 1030 says a family with no good person to prop it (அடுத்தூன்றும் நல்லாள் இலாத குடி) falls when trouble cuts at its foot. Both make a group's survival depend on a capable person at its head, in the army and in the household.
